newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada natgas market seen strong throughout 1997.
newsitem.headline: Canada natgas market seen strong throughout 1997.

text.p: Frigid temperatures across western Canada may be driving natural gas demand and prices skyward in the short term but several factors bode well for market strength for the rest of 1997, analysts say.
"I think there's been a fundamental change for the better and come spring, I don't see a major correction downwards," said Peter Linder, analyst with brokerage CIBC Wood Gundy.

Spot prices at the AECO storage hub in southeastern Alberta this week have jumped as high as C$3.50 per gigajoule for next-day delivery with temperatures in the province again forecast to drop by Thursday.

AECO prices hovered between C$1.35 and C$1.40 per GJ a year ago. One-year forward packages, a window into the industry's future price expectations, have also crept above C$2, up from C$1.58 last year.
Strong Canadian prices have mirrored those in the United States, where cold weather has stricken areas as far as the southern states and snowstorms have crippled the Midwest.

Apart from the cold weather, industry experts were surprised by the sharp drawdown in storage gas reported by the Canadian Gas Association last Friday. The most recent numbers were released following a two-week holiday break.
The CGA reported Canadian storage facilities were 58.52 percent full on January 3, up from 56.20 percent last year.

However, facilities in western Canada's producing region, where temperatures have been bone-chillingly cold for much of the last three months, were tapped to 51.56 percent of capacity, nearly nine percent below the same period in 1996.

"The fact that you started off the (gas year starting November 1) at a level 30 (billion cubic feet) above the previous year's level and by January 3, you're 20 BCF lower than the level of a year ago bodes extremely well for gas prices," said Linder, who projects an average AECO spot price of C$2 per GJ and corporate average price of C$2.25 in 1997.
"The way withdrawals are going, roughly 1.5 to 1.7 BCF per day, we'll like get down to a very low level come April 1."
Martin Molyneaux, analyst with FirstEnergy Capital Corp, said that if withdrawals continued at current rates, stocks would be depleted by the end of February.
Molyneaux recently boosted his 1997 spot price projection to C$1.75 per GJ, up 10 cents.
Adding to strong domestic demand for gas has been the resurgence of the California and U.S. Pacific Northwest markets, which have also been pulling much of Canada's supply.

Prices at Sumas on the British Columbia-Washington border, North America's most depressed market for much of 1995 and 1996, have been above US$3 per million British thermal units for several weeks and were quoted on Tuesday at US$4.09.
In January 1996, Sumas gas fetched a scant US$1.13 per mmBtu.

The strength in Califorina demand has also meant producers who contracted expensive expansion capacity on Pacific Gas Transmission's pipeline to California from B.C. in 1993 are finding it valuable for the first time, Molyneaux said.
Natural gas drilling and the bringing on of previously uneconomic wells was unlikely to stem the effects of a major draw on Alberta and B.C. gas supply in the short term, analysts said.
Today, producers are focusing more on oil development and exploratory gas drilling, keeping Canada's rig fleet near maximum activity, Linder said.

However, with record cash flows expected from Canadian producers in the fourth quarter of 1996 and first quarter of 1997 likely adding fuel to corporate budgets, the industry may risk drilling itself into a surplus situation again after spring trying to meet 1998 demand, Molyneaux said.
((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
